source.title: Interpreting Face Inference Models Using Hierarchical Network Dissection
source.authors: Divyang Teotia; Àgata Lapedriza; S. Ostadabbas

page_placements.theme: Neuron concept labels, selectivity and interpretability scores depend on the method

record.tranche_reason: The study compares two concept-pairing and interpretability measurements on trained vision models and reports that they produce different unit-concept results. It does not use the original neuron-activation examples or test whether the paired concepts are unrelated.
record.gate_note: The study measures units paired with facial concepts and compares Hierarchical Network Dissection with Network Dissection. Its results bear on how interpretation depends on scoring, but do not establish that units respond to unrelated inputs: many compared concepts overlap spatially or are related. Controlled-bias experiments report bias-discovery outcomes, not polysemanticity results, so they are not included as rows.
record.test_reason: This is an interpretability-method paper for face models. It compares its own Hierarchical Network Dissection with IoU-based Network Dissection on counts of interpretable units and unit-concept pairings. It never measures or classifies neurons as polysemantic, meaning responding to unrelated inputs. The multiple concepts a unit pairs with are, by design, spatially overlapping concepts in one facial region, such as 5 o'Clock Shadow and Rosy Cheeks. The method lets a unit carry several concepts, so the higher multi-concept counts come from the scoring rule, not from a test of polysemanticity. Every row compares the study's own method with a prior method on interpretable-unit coverage, which is a related but different construct. No version of the claim is tested.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors present Hierarchical Network Dissection and a Face Dictionary as a way to handle spatially overlapping and global concepts in face models. They argue it gives more complete interpretability reports than Network Dissection. They also claim the dissection reports reveal training-data biases, such as gender skew in the smile model, and show bias discovery in controlled experiments. The paraphrase omits this bias-discovery conclusion, which is a main contribution.
record.recipe_differences: The method is inspired by Network Dissection but adds probabilistic concept scoring and a staged hierarchy for global concepts, facial parts, and local concepts. It compares its reports with the original method.
record.method_sensitivity: Unit-concept results and reported coverage vary with the scoring/pairing method (hierarchical probabilistic scoring versus IoU-based Network Dissection).

fits_no_version.finding: Unit-concept labels and the share of interpretable units depend on the dissection scoring rule. Coverage is about 70-80% under the hierarchical probabilistic method versus about 50-60% under IoU-based Network Dissection. In one example, scoring changes the top concept of Unit 142.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: In vision CNNs, the concept assigned to a unit and the share of units judged interpretable depend on the concept-pairing scoring method.

fits_no_version.finding: Units often score highly for several spatially overlapping concepts in the same facial region. In the Eyeglasses bias experiment, the authors suggest units may be discriminative by facial region rather than by individual concept.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Units in face CNNs tend to respond to a facial region rather than to individual fine-grained attributes within it.

record.problems: The Face Dictionary is limited and the authors say this limits interpretability coverage. The method uses assumptions about exclusive global subgroups and lenient thresholds. Most figures do not give numerical values in the text. The authors caution that the coverage comparison is not strictly fair because the hierarchical method includes global concepts. The study does not establish that multiple paired concepts are unrelated.
record.rows_left_out: The layer-by-layer coverage values in Fig. 8 are not separately extracted; the text provides only an approximate aggregate for most non-FaceNet models. Controlled-bias experiment results in Sections 5.1-5.2 are excluded because they report bias discovery rather than unit polysemanticity or interpretation-scoring outcomes.

untested.parts: There is no test of single neurons responding to unrelated image inputs. Multi-concept pairings are restricted to related concepts within one facial region.
Superposition and capacity pressure are not examined.
Initialization, regularization and training-noise causes are not examined.
There is no manipulation of activation function or architecture aimed at reducing polysemanticity.
No canonical polysemantic neurons are re-examined.
Labels and coverage depend on the scoring rule, but the study never classifies neurons as polysemantic. It also does not vary the activation range examined beyond the method's fixed design.

record.verdict_notes: The reader linked all rows to V7 and labeled them supports or limits_scope. That link is not warranted: the paper measures interpretable-unit coverage and concept rankings, not polysemanticity. Its method is built to let a unit pair with several overlapping, related concepts, so multi-concept pairing is produced by the method rather than found. All rows are relinked to none, and no verdicts are given.

versions.untested_parts: The study does not test whether neurons respond to several unrelated image inputs.
No language models or transformer MLP neurons are studied.
The study does not test superposition or feature-to-neuron capacity pressure.
The study does not test initialization, regularization, or training noise as causes of polysemanticity.
The study does not compare activation functions or architectures as a means of reducing polysemanticity, or assess the associated performance cost.
The study does not investigate whether canonical mixtures of unrelated inputs share a coherent feature.
It compares concept-pairing methods, but does not vary the activation range examined or directly classify neurons as polysemantic.

rows.subject: GENDER ResNet-50, Unit 142
rows.operation_detail: Compared IoU-based Network Dissection with the hierarchical probability scoring for concepts in the Cheek Region.
rows.value: Hierarchical method: Rosy Cheeks probability 0.2276; 5 o'Clock Shadow probability 0.1884; Rosy Cheeks IoU 0.1109
rows.note: The two scoring approaches rank the concepts differently. The authors explain that concepts in the same facial region can be difficult for a unit to distinguish; this example does not show an unrelated mixture.
rows.check: Unit 142 is a single example where two scoring rules rank two related same-region concepts differently. It does not show a unit responding to unrelated inputs, and it does not show a polysemantic/monosemantic classification flipping.

relation.reason: The paper never tests polysemantic neurons. It only discusses units paired with more than one related concept, so 'discusses' fits better than the reader's guess of 'tests'.

tranche.reason: The paper presents its own dissection method and does not measure polysemanticity. Its multi-concept units are paired with related concepts in the same facial region, not unrelated inputs. The reader's guess of T2 is not warranted.

source_check.notes: Every row compares the study's own method with Network Dissection on interpretable-unit counts or concept scores. Only r7 and r8 have numbers in the text; the rest are figure-only. None measures polysemanticity, because multi-concept pairings are related, same-region face concepts. The 70-80% vs 50-60% coverage applies to most non-FaceNet face models, and the authors call the comparison not strictly fair.

statements.correction: Six face-inference CNNs: five ResNet-50/18 and one InceptionResNetV1 (FaceNet). Deeper layers (ResNet Block3-4). Most models other than FaceNet: roughly 70-80% coverage under Hierarchical Network Dissection and around 50-60% under Network Dissection (Sec. 4.3, Fig. 8.b). FairFace and Beauty: lowest coverage in Fig. 8, with very few layers reaching 50%. The authors say the direct coverage comparison is not strictly fair because Network Dissection cannot account for global concepts. Gender ResNet-50, unit 142, second-last conv layer: IoU ranks 5 o'Clock Shadow first (0.1914). Probability scoring ranks Rosy Cheeks first (0.2276 vs 0.1884), even though its IoU is lower (0.1109).
statements.problem: The 70-80% and 50-60% figures are in the text, but they are for face-inference CNNs, not vision CNNs in general. They cover only 'most' of the models other than FaceNet, and FairFace and Beauty have the lowest coverage. The authors say the coverage comparison is not strictly fair, because Network Dissection cannot handle global concepts. In the example, the top concept changes between two related Cheek-Region concepts.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: Compared concept-pairing methods on the tested face models and deeper layers
reader_labels.reason: The methods yield different unit-concept rankings and coverage; the hierarchical method reports more interpretable units per concept and higher stated coverage (r1-r8).

reader_labels.label: limits_scope
reader_labels.condition: Coverage comparison between Hierarchical Network Dissection and Network Dissection
reader_labels.reason: The authors say the coverage comparison is not strictly fair because the hierarchical method includes global concepts that the original method cannot assess; the study also does not vary activation range (r8).
